introduction: On this Sunday, Isaiah speaks of the suffering servant who gives his life as an offering for sin. In the Gospel, James and John ask for the places of honor, and Jesus teaches that whoever wants to be great must be a servant, for the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. Hebrews tells us that we have a high priest who sympathizes with our weakness. Let us draw near to the throne of grace.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, we have a great high priest who understands our weakness. Let us approach the throne of grace with confidence.
intentions: For the Church, and especially for missionaries: that she may serve the world after the example of Christ. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who hold power in nations and communities: that they may use it to serve, not to dominate. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who serve others in hidden ways, at home, in hospitals and in care homes: that God may strengthen and reward them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are tempted and weak: that they may find mercy and grace in their time of need. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may seek greatness only in service. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord Jesus, you came not to be served but to serve, and to give your life for many. Make us servants of one another, and bring us to share your glory. You live and reign for ever and ever.

reflection.title: Not to be served but to serve
reflection.body:
James and John come to Jesus with a bold request: "Grant to us that we may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left hand, in your glory." They have just heard Jesus speak of his coming suffering, and they are thinking of thrones.

Jesus answers patiently: "You don't know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink?" They say they can. Jesus tells them that they will indeed share his cup, but that places of honor are not his to give.

The other ten are angry, and Jesus gathers them all. He contrasts two kinds of power. Among the nations, rulers "lord it over" their people. "But it shall not be so among you, but whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant." Then he gives the reason, which sums up his whole life: "For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."

Isaiah's suffering servant points in the same direction. "When you make his soul an offering for sin, he will see his offspring." Through his suffering, "My righteous servant will justify many."

The Letter to the Hebrews tells us what kind of high priest this servant is: "we don't have a high priest who can't be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin." And so it invites us: "Let's therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace."

This week, notice where you want to be first, recognized or in control. Then look for a small way to serve without being noticed. And when you feel weak, draw near to Jesus with confidence: he understands.
